references.text: Moses, Aaron, Nadab, Abihu, and seventy of the elders of Israel went up the mountain, which is the immediate context for the vision of the God of Israel.
God says that no one can see his face and live, but Moses saw his back. This illuminates the limits of human ability to see God.
Ezekiel sees God's throne with the appearance of sapphire stone, and a figure resembling a man seated on the throne. The sapphire description is directly parallel.
Ezekiel again sees something resembling sapphire stone, shaped like a throne, above the heads of the cherubim. The sapphire motif is repeated in the theophany.
Jacob saw God face to face at Peniel and survived. This is another account of seeing God directly.
Isaiah saw the Lord sitting on a high and lofty throne. This is another prophetic vision of God's throne.
John sees a throne in heaven, and the one seated on it resembles jasper and carnelian. The gemstone motif in the throne vision has parallels to the sapphire in Exodus.
The foundations of the new Jerusalem are adorned with precious stones, including sapphire. Sapphire is associated with God's dwelling place and glory.
Those who are pure in heart shall see God. This promise to see God connects to the elders' experience at Sinai.
Complementary descriptions of the same event at Sinai: God's purity (sapphire stone) contrasted with his awe-inspiring power (fire).
Theological parallel between God's presence at Sinai and in the new creation, both described through clarity and precious stones (sapphire stone/jasper).
Ezekiel's vision of the sapphire-like expanse (1:26) is the direct prophetic explanation of what Moses saw under God's feet in Exodus 24:10.
Theological contrast between God's heavenly 'work' of sapphire stone and the enemy's contemptuous reference to God's 'work' as human craftsmanship.
